networking-essentials.text: The phone asks DNS for the address, then sends the request to a load balancer, which passes it to one app server. The server reads the database and the answer travels back the same way.
Every round trip pays for distance. Images and pages that rarely change are served from a CDN near the user, so most of the bytes never cross the country.
A server can stop answering at any moment. The load balancer stops sending to it, and clients retry with a growing wait, so a hiccup does not turn into a flood.

caching.text: Zotato’s menus are read thousands of times a second at dinner and changed a few times a day. Without a cache, each read is a database query of tens of milliseconds.

words: Most reads stop at the cache
caching.text: The app asks the cache first and goes to the database only on a miss. With 90% of reads answered from memory, the database sees a tenth of the traffic.
Memory is small. An eviction policy decides what leaves: usually the entry used least recently, because what was read a minute ago will probably be read again.
When a popular entry expires, every request misses together and hits the database in the same second. Refresh it a little early, or let one request rebuild it while the rest wait.

sharding.text: First prove you need it: one machine can hold a lot. Shard only when the data or the writes outgrow the biggest machine you can buy.

words: Split the rows by a key
sharding.text: A shard key decides where each row lives. The router reads the key and sends the request to the one shard that holds it.
Shard by city, and Mumbai lands on one machine while the others idle. A good key spreads both data and traffic evenly.
A query that needs rows from every shard asks all of them and waits for the slowest. Choose the key so the common queries stay on one shard.

consistent-hashing.text: Send each key to hash(key) mod 3 and the load is even. Add a fourth server and the answer changes for almost every key: most of the cache is suddenly in the wrong place.

words: A key goes to the next one
consistent-hashing.text: Hash servers and keys onto the same circle. Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from it.
A new node takes over one arc. Only the keys on that arc move; every other key stays where it was.

cap-theorem.text: The same data lives in two cities so either can answer. Every write reaches both copies over the link between them.
Networks fail. While the copies cannot talk, a write in Mumbai cannot reach Delhi. Each copy can either refuse, or answer with what it has.
For a bank balance or the last seat on a flight, the cut-off copy refuses until the link is back. Some users get an error, nobody gets a wrong answer.
For a like count or a menu, both copies keep answering and catch up later. Everyone gets an answer, some see an older one for a while.

api-design.text: The path says which resource, the query says how to narrow or shape the answer, and the body carries the data being created or changed.

words: An idempotency key stops a double order
api-design.text: Only POST, and some PATCHes, change the outcome when sent twice. Placing an order carries a key, so the second copy returns the first answer.
One query for the list and one per order makes 51. A batching loader collects the 50 restaurant ids and fetches them together: 2 in all.

data-modelling.text: List what each main screen reads and writes, then draw the tables, their keys and how they link. The shape decides which reads are one lookup.

words: Then decide how far to normalise
data-modelling.text: Add the indexes that serve the main screens, and keep each fact in one place unless a hot read needs a copy.

words: A key-value store for hot reads
data-modelling.text: The relational database stays the source of truth; a key-value store in front of it serves the hot reads. A change updates the database and removes the cached copy.

database-indexing.text: To find one phone number, the database reads the table page by page until it finds the row.
Looking up id 350: the root says between 300 and 600, an internal page narrows it to 340 to 360, and the leaf points to the row. The top levels stay in memory.
A new order updates the table and each of its three indexes before the insert is done. Index what you read, not everything.

words: Does more than old figures say
numbers-to-know.text: A single cloud machine today has many cores, terabytes of memory when optimised for it, tens of terabytes of local SSD and a fast network.

words: About ten times the one before
numbers-to-know.text: Memory, SSD, a call in the same zone, another zone, another region: each step is roughly ten times slower than the one before.

words: Shard when the numbers say so
numbers-to-know.text: Zotato’s users and a year of orders fit on one large database many times over. Sharding makes sense only for many years of history or far higher write rates.

real-time-updates.text: Polling asks again and again and learns of a message up to one interval late. Long polling keeps the request waiting so the answer leaves the moment the message arrives.
From the chat service to the connection server holding Ravi’s open connection, then down that connection to his phone.
Server-sent events push down one open response and resume from the last id after a cut. A WebSocket lets either side send whenever it has something.

words: Read then write leaves a gap
contention.text: Both requests read “1 left”, both write “sold”. In the gap between the read and the write, another request read the same value.
Update the row only if the seat is still free. The database applies it one request at a time, so exactly one buyer wins and the other is told no.
A hold with an expiry needs nobody to release it, so an app that crashes mid-payment can’t keep the seat forever.

words: One request can’t do it all
workflows.text: Payment, the restaurant and dispatch each take their own time and can fail on their own. One request that waits for all of them breaks halfway.

words: One state, a few allowed moves
workflows.text: Every order is in exactly one state. The table of allowed moves rules out the impossible ones, like accepting an order that was already cancelled.
The engine records each finished step. When a worker dies, a new one replays the history to learn which steps are done and what they returned.

scaling-reads.text: Find out how many reads there really are and which ones. A missing index or an extra query often costs more than any new layer.
Each layer answers what it can and passes on the rest. Of 1 lakh reads a second, 400 reach the primary database.
A hot key turns one expired entry into a flood. Coalescing sends one request to the database, and a short copy in each server spreads the reads.

words: Every one lands on the primary
scaling-writes.text: Reads can be copied and cached; writes can’t. Each one must reach the one primary that owns the row.

words: A queue keeps the pace steady
scaling-writes.text: The queue turns a 10-minute spike into a 34-minute stretch of steady writing. Nothing is lost, and the database never goes past what it can take.
Ten parts on five shards turn one overloaded key into ten easy ones. A read adds ten numbers instead of reading one.

big-files.text: A 1.6 GB video sent through the API ties up an app server for the whole upload, and one dropped connection means starting again.
The server only signs the upload. The phone sends parts straight to storage, so a dropped connection costs one 100 MB part, not the whole 1.6 GB.
Storage holds the bytes, but only the database row says whether a file is safe to show. Downloads are served from a CDN near the user.

long-jobs.text: The API records the job, puts it on a queue and answers at once with an id. Workers take jobs from the queue at their own pace.
A lease is a promise with an expiry. Renewals keep it while the worker is healthy; if it goes quiet, the job goes to someone else.
Growing waits give a struggling service room to recover, and after the last try the dead-letter queue takes the job out of the way.

nearby-search.text: An index on latitude finds a long strip, an index on longitude another. Near me is neither: the database still filters a lot of rows.
The map is cut into cells with short names. Every extra character divides a cell into 32, so the length you index decides how many cells a search touches.

words: Splits only where it is busy
nearby-search.text: A fixed grid wastes cells on empty land and overloads the busy centre. A quadtree splits only where the restaurants are.

words: Close in meaning, close in space
vector-search.text: An embedding turns text into a point. Keyword search needs shared words; embeddings need shared meaning. That is why cottage cheese finds paneer.

words: A few hundred checked, not crores
vector-search.text: An approximate index trades a little accuracy for a huge saving: it checks a few hundred vectors instead of crores.

words: Data that arrives by the clock
time-series.text: Rider locations, metrics and prices arrive every few seconds, almost never change, and are read as “the last hour”.
Points from one series are similar to their neighbours, so storing only what changed shrinks them about tenfold.

words: Keep less detail as it ages
time-series.text: Dashboards rarely need ten-second detail from last year. Summaries keep the shape of old data at a fraction of the cost.

sketches.text: Counting distinct users exactly means remembering every id you have seen. At crores of users a day, that set is huge.

words: Distinct counts in a small fixed space
sketches.text: The longest run of zeros in a hash is a noisy clue to how many distinct items were hashed; averaging thousands of such clues makes it precise.
Collisions can only add to a counter, never subtract, so the smallest of an item’s counters is the closest to the truth.

words: One of the writes will fail
change-capture.text: The service writes the database, then the search index and the cache. When the second write fails, they disagree and nothing notices.
The log already has every committed change, in order, and is how replicas stay in step. CDC reads it and publishes each change to a stream.
A snapshot gives a new consumer the present, and the log position taken with it makes sure every change after that is delivered.

redis.text: Strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets. Every command changes one structure in one step, so a cart, a ranking or a rate limit needs no locks.
Memory is lost on a restart. Redis can save snapshots and an append-only log to disk; how often decides how much you can lose.
The client knows which node owns each slot, so a request takes one hop; a MOVED reply corrects it after slots change hands.

words: Each search reads its own lists
elasticsearch.text: The index is built once per change; every search then reads only the lists for its own words. That is why searching crores of dishes takes milliseconds.

words: One source of truth, a stream of changes
elasticsearch.text: Never write the database and the index from the same request and hope both succeed. Feed the index from a stream of the database’s changes.
An index is split into shards with replicas. New documents become searchable after the next refresh, so search is a little behind the database.

words: Same key, same partition, in order
kafka-in-practice.text: An order’s events carry its id as the key, so they land on one partition and stay in order. Order holds within a partition, not across the topic.

words: Up to one consumer per partition
kafka-in-practice.text: The group decides who reads what. Adding a consumer is how you scale reading, up to one per partition: a fourth consumer on three partitions sits idle.
Events wait in the log while consumers catch up. Watch the lag, add consumers up to the partition count, and make each one faster.

temporal.text: Workers run your code and report each step. The service records it, so losing a worker loses nothing.
The history tells the next worker which steps are done and what they returned. The workflow continues as if nothing happened.

words: Costs a row, not a thread
temporal.text: Timers and signals are stored in the service, not in a sleeping thread. A workflow waiting a day for a refund costs a row in a database.

api-gateways.text: The gateway checks who is calling, whether they may, whether they are within their limit, and where the request goes. A customer’s order passes and reaches Orders.
A restaurant’s billing system that sends too many requests is stopped at the limit check and told to slow down, before it reaches any service.
Every request passes the gateway, so it is the natural place to send a small share to a new version and to undo that if it misbehaves.

words: The partition key is the address
cassandra.text: A query that gives the partition key goes to the three nodes that own it. There is no leader: any node can take the request.
A query that doesn’t give the partition key goes to all of them. Model one table per question so every query has its key.
Without a leader, a delete must be remembered for a while, or a replica that missed it would bring the row back. That memory is the tombstone.

dynamodb.text: Design the keys from the questions: partition key customer, sort key time, and “my recent orders” is one query.

words: No matching key means a scan
dynamodb.text: An index keyed by restaurant answers “this kitchen’s orders”. A question with no matching key is a scan.

words: Fixed in the key, not with capacity
dynamodb.text: The table’s total capacity hides a per-partition limit. A key everyone writes to is throttled; the fix is in the key design.

postgresql.text: A long report and a stream of price changes don’t wait for each other. The price is old versions that vacuum has to clean up.

words: A few dozen busy, not thousands idle
postgresql.text: PostgreSQL wants a few dozen busy connections. A pooler is the usual answer once there are many app servers.
Replicas follow the primary’s log and serve reads. If the primary fails, one is promoted and the app reconnects to it.

flink.text: Arrival order is an accident of the network. Counting by when events happened, with a watermark to decide when to stop waiting, gives the same answer every time.
Saving every task’s state and the input positions at the same logical moment is what makes a replay consistent.
The job reloads the last checkpoint and rereads the input from the saved positions. The counts come out the same.

zookeeper.text: A write is safe once a majority has it. Reads are local and fast, which is why they can lag a little.
Each candidate watches the one just before it. A leader’s death wakes one waiting worker, not all of them.

shopify-reservations.text: Holds lived in Redis and stock in MySQL. With no transaction across the two, a failure between them could leave a hold without stock or stock without a hold.
Each row is one unit for sale. A checkout locks the rows it takes, and SKIP LOCKED makes the next checkout pass over them to free ones instead of waiting.
When checkouts slowed, the queries were fine. The time went on getting a database connection, so the fix was in connection handling.

discord-messages.text: The message store kept growing, and hot channels made some nodes fall behind. Running it took more and more of the team.
Requests for one channel go to the same data service instance. The first starts one query and the rest wait for its answer, so a burst becomes one read.

words: Trillions of messages in nine days
discord-messages.text: With the data service in place, the messages were copied to ScyllaDB in nine days and the cluster became far calmer to run.

slack-job-queue.text: During an outage the queue grew until Redis ran out of memory. Then nothing could be queued, or even taken off the queue.
Kafka takes jobs as fast as the web app sends them and keeps the backlog on disk. A relay feeds Redis only as fast as its rate limit allows.

figma-multiplayer.text: Figma skipped operational transforms. Every change goes through one server, which decides the order everyone sees.
Changes to different properties never conflict. When two edits change the same property, the one that reaches the server last wins.

words: A chain of reads per file
spotify-data-lake.text: Without an index, every file needs a chain of reads, each waiting for the last, so a lookup by key in the lake is slow.

words: A few small reads, all at once
spotify-data-lake.text: Random Access Parquet keeps an index from each key to its files and rows; the ranged reads then go out together, without copying data into a key-value store.

meta-zgateway.text: More than a million client hosts connected straight to the database hosts they needed, so each host’s connections grew with the number of clients.
Clients connect to their regional ZGateway, and database hosts see only the gateways. It is also one place to batch, merge duplicate reads and shed load.
